parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Apparatus used to produce stationary waves on a stretched string is shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

Fig. 7.1

The frequency generator is switched on.
parts.text: Describe two adjustments that can be made to the apparatus to produce stationary waves on the string.

markscheme_points.text: alter distance from vibrator to pulley; alter frequency of generator; (change tension in string by) changing value of the masses; any two

hints: Hint 1: Think about why a stationary wave only appears for certain fits of the wavelength on the string, and what parts of Fig. 7.1 you are free to move or change.
Hint 2: Focus on the three things that control the wavelength and wave speed: the vibrating length, the driving frequency, and the tension set by the hanging masses.
parts.proper_answer: Adjust the distance between vibrator and pulley and adjust the frequency of the generator (or adjust the tension by changing the hanging masses) until resonance is obtained. Any two.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why tuning is needed**
A stationary wave forms only when the reflected wave from the pulley overlaps exactly with the incoming wave to give resonance. That happens when the length $L$ fits a whole number of half-wavelengths. At most random settings you just see a blur.

Step 2: **What you can change**
You can change $L$ by sliding the vibrator to alter the distance to the pulley. You can change the driving frequency $f$ on the frequency generator. You can change the wave speed $v$ by changing the tension $T$ with different masses, since $$v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$ Any two of these adjustments will let you find resonance.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Describe the features that are seen on the stretched string that indicate stationary waves have been produced.

markscheme_points.text: points on string have amplitudes varying from maximum to zero/minimum

hints: Hint 1: Picture the string shape at resonance - some points never move at all while points halfway between them swing the most.
parts.proper_answer: Fixed points of zero amplitude (nodes) separated by points of maximum amplitude (antinodes).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Nodes and antinodes**
In a progressive wave every point vibrates with the same amplitude. In a stationary wave the amplitude depends on position. At nodes the two opposite waves always cancel, so displacement is always zero. At antinodes midway between nodes they always reinforce, so vibration has maximum amplitude. Seeing this regular max-to-zero pattern proves a stationary wave is present.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Determine the phase difference between wave R and wave S. Include an appropriate unit.
hints: Hint 1: Pick the same feature on both curves, for example the upward zero crossing, and compare how much later S does it than R relative to one full period $T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the common period**
Both R and S repeat every $$T = 0.60 \text{ s}$$ For example R crosses zero going up at $t = 0$ and again at $t = 0.60 \text{ s}$. S crosses zero going up at $t = 0.10 \text{ s}$ and again at $t = 0.70 \text{ s}$.

Step 2: **Convert time lag to phase**
The time lag is $$\Delta t = 0.10 \text{ s}$$ Phase difference $\phi$ is the fraction of a cycle times a full cycle: $$\phi = \frac{\Delta t}{T} \times 360^{\circ} = \frac{0.10}{0.60} \times 360^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}$$ This is the same as $\pi/3 \text{ rad}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Calculate the ratio

$$\frac{\text{intensity of wave R}}{\text{intensity of wave S}}.$$
hints: Hint 1: Read the peak heights of R and S from Fig. 7.2 and remember that for waves of the same frequency, the brighter or louder wave is the one with larger amplitude.
Hint 2: Use the proportionality for intensity $I$ with amplitude $A$ at constant frequency to form the squared ratio of the two amplitudes.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the amplitudes**
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. From the graph: $$A_R = 3.4 \text{ cm}$$ $$A_S = 2.2 \text{ cm}$$ Both have the same frequency because both have period $0.60 \text{ s}$.

Step 2: **Apply intensity law**
For the same medium and frequency, intensity $I$ is proportional to (amplitude)$^2$: $$I \propto A^2$$ So the ratio cancels the constants: $$\frac{I_R}{I_S} = \left(\frac{A_R}{A_S}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{3.4}{2.2}\right)^2 \approx 2.4$$
